status: PUB-9C PASS-03 BATCH 2 — VERIFIED AUTHORITY EXPANSION
policy: Metadata verified against PubMed, PMC, Nature, Annual Reviews, or equivalent publisher-level records. These authorities support only the exact burdens identified below; they do not establish civilization-scale organismhood.

records.citation: Estes, Lyndon, Paul R. Elsen, Timothy Treuer, Labeeb Ahmed, Kelly Caylor, Jason Chang, Jonathan J. Choi, and Erle C. Ellis. 2018. ‘The Spatial and Temporal Domains of Modern Ecology.’ Nature Ecology & Evolution 2: 819–826. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-018-0524-4.
records.whatThisSourceSupports: Observation scale must distinguish temporal resolution/interval from observation duration/extent; phenomena can be mischaracterized when observed over inappropriate scales.
records.whatThisSourceDoesNotSupport: It does not support the existence of a hidden organism or imply that scale mismatch is evidence of life.
records.whereMacroscopicLifeGoesBeyondIt: Macroscopic Life turns scale mismatch into a methodological caution inside a larger adversarial test architecture.

records.citation: Glazier, Douglas S. 2023. ‘The Relevance of Time in Biological Scaling.’ Biology 12 (8): 1084. https://doi.org/10.3390/biology12081084.
records.whatThisSourceSupports: Biological rates and durations occur across different temporal scales, and no single universal biological clock should be assumed.
records.whatThisSourceDoesNotSupport: It does not establish any universal scaling exponent, hidden macroscopic life cycle, or civilization-scale organism.
records.whereMacroscopicLifeGoesBeyondIt: Macroscopic Life uses temporal scale as one observer-window dimension while explicitly refusing to infer life from slowness alone.

records.citation: Gabaldón, Toni. 2021. ‘Origin and Early Evolution of the Eukaryotic Cell.’ Annual Review of Microbiology 75: 631–647. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-micro-090817-062213.
records.whatThisSourceSupports: The origin of mitochondria from alphaproteobacterial endosymbiosis is a robustly established event in eukaryotic evolution, while important details of timing, host identity, and early interaction remain debated.
records.whatThisSourceDoesNotSupport: It does not imply that modern social or technological integration follows the mitochondrial route or that endosymbiosis is a universal transition template.
records.whereMacroscopicLifeGoesBeyondIt: Macroscopic Life uses mitochondrial integration as a precedent and calibration case, not as a diagnosis of civilization.

records.citation: Rainey, Paul B., and Silvia De Monte. 2014. ‘Resolving Conflicts During the Evolutionary Transition to Multicellular Life.’ Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics 45: 599–620. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-ecolsys-120213-091740.
records.whatThisSourceSupports: Conflict among lower-level units is central to transitions in individuality, and mechanisms that alter or resolve conflict can contribute to higher-level Darwinian organization.
records.whatThisSourceDoesNotSupport: It does not establish that every cooperative collective becomes an individual or that social conflict-control mechanisms are biologically equivalent to multicellular mechanisms.
records.whereMacroscopicLifeGoesBeyondIt: Macroscopic Life converts conflict-control precedent into one component of a multi-test, dependence-aware higher-order individuality framework.

records.citation: Xiao, Yang, Tijs Louwies, Ruben A. T. Mars, and Purna C. Kashyap. 2024. ‘The Human Microbiome—A Physiologic Perspective.’ Comprehensive Physiology 14 (3): 5491–5519. https://doi.org/10.1002/cphy.c230013.
records.whatThisSourceSupports: Human-associated microbes occupy multiple body systems, their metabolites and interactions can shape host physiological functions, and microbiome composition is dynamic and context-dependent.
records.whatThisSourceDoesNotSupport: It does not settle the philosophical or evolutionary boundary of the human individual and does not imply that all host-associated microbes form one evolutionary individual with the host.
records.whereMacroscopicLifeGoesBeyondIt: Macroscopic Life uses the microbiome to show that biologically meaningful boundaries can be relational and plural without treating that complexity as proof of higher-order individuality elsewhere.
